*323. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Nagpur has been ranked at the 
lowest level i.e. 18th while Pune is on 1st position on the food 
38 

[12 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
security index in the Food Insecurity Atlas of Urban India compiled by 
Swaminathan Research Foundation in collaboration with the World Food 
Programme; and 
(b) if so, what steps Government propose to take to erasure that food 
security (an essential input) is maintained at comparatively even levels atleast 
in metropolitan cities to begin with, with provision to gradually eliminate 
insecurity in food level all over the country? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS. FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) Yes. Sir. 
(b) The following steps have been taken by the Government of lndia to 
promote food security:— 
(i) Sufficient buffer stocks of foodgrains are maintained on a year-
round basis in keeping with the prescribed Minimum Buffer 
stocking norms for food security so that, among other things, 
emergent situations arising out of unexpected crop failure, 
natural disasters, etc. can be met. 
(ii) Distribution of foodgrains under the Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) is done through a vast distribution 
network of about 4.60 lakh Fair Price Shops (FPSs), of which 
around 72,000 FPSs are located in urban areas, including in 
metropolitan cities. The Central Government has been making 
allocation of foodgrains under the TPDS to the State 
Governments and Union Terri tory Administrations for 
distribution to Below Poverty Line (BPL) and Above Poverty 
Line families at the rate of 35 kg. per family per month at 
subsidized rates. 
(iii) The thrust in the TPDS is to include the really poor and 
vulnerable sections of the society, not only in the rural areas, 
but also slum dwellers and persons earning their livelihood, on 
daily basis, like porters, rickshaw-pullers, hand-cart pullers and 
fruit and flower sellers on the pavements in urban areas. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
(iv) In order to address the needs of the one crore poorest of the poor 
families, the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) is being 
Implemented in al! parts of the country under which foodgrains 
are issued at the highly subsidized price of Rs. 2 per kg. for 
wheat and Rs. 3 per kg, for rice. 
(v) Foodgrains are also being allocated under various Welfare 
Schemes like the Mid-Day Meal Scheme and Annapurna 
Scheme. 
(vi) Financial empowerment through provision of gainful 
employment is a major vehicle for ensuring food security, as it 
enable the family to purchase its requirements from the open 
market. The Sampoorna Gramin Rojgar Yojana (SGRY) 
provides both wage employment and foodgrains in rural areas. In 
urban areas, schemes such as the Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar 
Yojana (SJSRY) are under implementation for providing self-
employment and wage-employment to the urban poor.

likely to arise by linking the pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme,

Statement 
Steps taken by the Government to promote the Information 
Technology Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been 
rationalised and extended uniformly to all sectors without any 
threshold limit on payment of 5%. 
71 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to the 
Information Technology sector, with the exception of Business-to-
consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Electronics Hardware Technology  Park (EHTP) and Software 
Technology Park (STP) Schemes are implemented under the aegis 
of the Department of Information Technology, Ministry of 
Communications and Information Technology, through a single 
window mechanism of the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee 
(IMSC). 
4. Supplies of Information Technol ogy Agreement (ITA-1) items in 
the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) by EHTP/EOU/EPZ units shall be 
counted towards fulfilment of minimum Net Foreign Exchange 
earning as a Percentage of exports (NFEP) and the minimum 
Export Performance (EP), provided that the items are manufactured 
in the unit and attract zero rate of basic customs duty. Positive 
NFEP is required to be achieved in 5 years instead of every year. 
5. DTA access upto 50% of the FOB value of export is permitted for 
electronics hardware units under EOU/EPZ/EHTP schemes and the 
software units under EOU/EPZ/STP schemes. 
6. Accelerated depreciation norms extended to computers and 
computer peripherals to all units and capital goods of IT hardware 
units under Export Oriented schemes (EOU/EPZ/STP/EHTP). 
These shall stand depreciated to overall limit of 90% over a period 
of 3 years. 
7. Special Economic Zones are being set up to enable hassles free 
manufacturing and trading for export purposes. 
8. The depreciation on Computers is allowed @ 60%. 
9. In the Budget 2002-03, the peak rate of customs duty has been 
reduced from 35% to 30%. Customs duty has been reduced on 
stepper motors for computers/pr inters from 5% of 0%, floppy 
diskette and unrecorded magnetic tape from 15% to 10%, ink 
cartridges/ribbon assembly/ribbon gear assembly/ribbon gear

Statement-II 
Criteria for upgradation of branch post offices in the country 
(a) In Rural Areas: 
The minimum work load of the Extra Departmental Branch Post Office, 
proposed to be upgraded, should be five hours per day. The permissible 
limit of annual loss is Rs. 2400/- in Normal Rural areas and Rs. 4800/- in 
Tribal and hilly areas. 
(b) In Urban Areas:  
In Urban areas, the post office should initially be self-supporting and at 
the time of the first annual review, it should show a 5% profit to be 
eligible for further retention. 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 Kms. in 
cities with a population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms. In other 
Urban Areas. No two-delivery offices, however, should be closer than 5 
Kms. for each other. 
Heads of Circles have powers to relax the distance condition in 10% of the 
cases. 
A Delivery Post Office in Urban Area should have a minimum of 7 
Postmen's beats.

(b) (i) Rice and wheat 
With the introduction of TPDS from June, 1997 the allocation of 
foodgrains to States\UTs is made as per TPDS guidelines. The quantity of 
foodgrains for families below the poverty line (BPL) has been increased from 
initial 10 kg. per family per month to 20 kg. from April, 2000; to 25 kg. from 
July, 2001 and to 35kg. from April, 2002. 
The allocation for families above the poverty line (APL) which was being 
made on historical basis has also ben fixed @ 35 kg. per APL family per 
month from April, 2002. Allocation to Antyodaya families which was fixed at 25 
kg. per family per month at the time of implementation of Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana in March, 2001, has been increased to 35 kg. per family per month from 
April, 2002. 
The allocation underTPDS was made as per the number of estimated families 
on the basis of population estimates of 1995. From 1 -12-2000 the population base 
was revised to the population projection of the Rigistrar General as on 1-3-
2000. 
(ii) Sugar 
The monthly levy sugar quotas are allocated on uniform norms and not on 
the basis of demand or reuests received from State Governments. From January, 
1996 till February, 2000 the allocation is made @ 425 grams per person per 
month for tiie population as per 1991 census. From March, 2000 the population 
base was revised as per population projections of 1 -3-2000. The quantity of sugar 
allocated was increased from 425 grams to 500 grams per person per month from 
July 2000. In the case of following 16 States/UTs the levy sugar quota is allotted 
on higher per capita availability in view of the special circumstances in these 
States/UTs:- 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigrah, Assam, 
Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Lakshadweep, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Sikkim, Pondicherry, Tripura, Jammu & Kashmir and Uttaranchal. 
With the reducation of levy obligation from 40% to 30% with effect from 
1.1.2000, the income tax assessees and their family members were excluded from 
the purview of the PDS sugar from July, 2000. Government

RAJU): (a) Yes, Sir. A Statement showing State-wise quantity of levy rice and 
paddy procured by the FCI from Kharif Marketing Season 1997-98 to 2001 -02 
is enclosed (See below). 
(b) and (c) The present policy of MSP and procurement of FAQ 
standard of foodgrains is being implemented with the help of the State 
Governments unifonnly in all States, which have potential for procurement. This 
policy has been successful in meeting the purpose of ensuring MSP to the 
farmers. 
With a view to effecting savings in the form of reduction in the outgo 
of food subsidy, enhancing the effi ciency of procurement and PDS and 
encouraging local procurement to the maximum extent thereby extending the 
benefits of MSP to local farmers, the scheme of Decentralized Procurement 
of Foodgrains was introduced by the Government in 1997-98. The scheme is 
now in operation in the States of West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Tamil Nadu and Uttaranchal. The Union Government 
has been encouraging States to adopt the scheme of Decentralized 
Procurement of Foodgrains. 
The difference between the economic cost of the State Government and the 
Central Issue Prices is passed on to the State Government as subsidy.

2246. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state:

become redundant due to the overflowing granaries of food in the country; 
(b) whether Government are planning to dismantle the Public 
Distribution System; 
(c) whether Govemment are planning to repeal the Essential 
Commodities Act so that the foodgrains can be moved freely from one State 
to the others; 
(d) whether Government are trying to monetise BPL, PDS cards for 
cash, or food stamps instead of grain; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof as to how Government are planning to 
organise the same?

AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI U. V. 
KRISHNAM RAJU): (a) and (b) No, Sir. 
(c) The Central Government have Issued an Order on 15.2.2002 under 
the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 allowing dealers to freely buy, stock, 
sell, transport, distribute, dispose, acquire, use or consume any quantity in 
respect of wheat, paddy/rice, coarse grains, sugar, edible oilseeds and edible 
oils without requiring any license or permit therefore under any order issued 
under the Act. 
(d) and (e) No, Sir. Questions do not arise.

Diversion of foodgrains by FCI 
2250. DR. ALLADI R RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the findings of the probe into diversion of wheat meant for the 
consumers to the traders by the Food Corporation of India In Haryana; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
(b) the details of the modus operandi of the scandal; 
(c) the quantity and value of wheat diverted to traders, the Monetary loss 
suffered by FCI and the estimated profits made by the traders by selling this 
wheat at exorbitant prices; and 
(d) the action taken against the concerned officials? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUIVIER 
AFFAIRS. FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI U.V. KRISHNAM 
RAJU): (a) to (d) Food Corporation of India (FCI) sold a total quantity of 29.14 
lakh MT of wheat in the open market at prefixed rates in Haryana during 
October, 1993 to April, 1997. With a view to ensuring that the wheat sold in the 
open market was made available to the local people, the stocks were released to 
traders after obtaining an affidavit from them to the effect that they would not sell 
the stock outside the revenue districts to which they belonged. These traders 
sold the stocks to other parties within the same revenue districts. The buyers of 
wheat through this second sale, who were technically not bound to the affidavit 
given by original buyers, sold the stocks of wheat to parties outside the States. 
The officers of the FCI were suspected to be involved in the above 
diversion of wheat to the open market and the matter was referred to Central 
Bureau of Investigation (CBI) who have completed their investigation in all the 
six cases registered in this behalf. CBI have already filed chargesheet in the 
appropriate Court of Law in two of the cases and closed one case- In the 
remaining three as recommended by CBI, disciplinary action has been 
initiated. However, in one case no action could be taken against an officer who 
had already been dismissed. The FCI did not incur any financial losses on this 
account since wheat under the Open Market Sale Scheme (Domestic) was sold 
at rates fixed by the Government from time to time.

Sluggishness in sugarcane prices 
 2265. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state; 
(a) whether the rising unsold stocks of sugar and also rising 
sugarcane arrears promised by the respective State Governments 
have resulted in lower sugar prices; 
(b) if so, whether it is feared that around 30 per cent less sugarcane would 
be sown by farmers because of consistent sluggish prices; 
(c) whether this has prompted the farmers to shift to other paying crops; 
and 
(d) if so, what are the concrete remedial measures Government propose 
to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION {SHRI U.V. KRISHNAM 
RAJU); (a) to (d) Due to higher level of production during the last four sugar 
seasons, there has been an accumulation of sugar stocks with the sugar 
factories. This has resulted in financial constraints to the sugar factories and 
the consequent increase in cane price dues of the farmers. Further, many mills 
have obtained the orders from the Courts for sale of sugar over and above 
their normal free sale quotas, due to which the prices of sugar have declined 
in the open market. 
So far, no report has been received from any quarter regarding 
reduction in sugarcane area and shifting of sugarcane by the farmers to some 
other cash crops. 
143 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
However, the Government has decided to create a buffer stock of 20 
lakh tonnes of sugar for a period of one year. This will enable the sugar mills 
to get a subsidy amount of Rs. 412 crore from the Sugar Development Fund. 
In addition, an amount of Rs. 374 crores would be available from the banks to 
the mills on account of buffer stock. Thus, a total amount of Rs. 786 crores 
would be provided to the mills enabling them to clear the payment of cane price 
dues to the sugarcane growers. This will also help the sugar industry to 
mitigate the financial hardship.

other law for the time being in force, where a fugitive criminal, who has

2329. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the PRIME MINISTER

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) A report on Foreign 
Investhient prepared by a Committee appointed by the Planning Commission 
and submitted to the Prime Minister has proposed some measures to attract 
more FDI into the country which include the following: 
• Consider the enactment of a Foreign Investment Promotion Law that 
incorporates and integrates aspects relevant to promotion of FDI. 
• Urge States to enact a special investment law relating to 
Infrastructure to expedite all investment in infrastructure sectors and 
remove hurdles to production in this critical sector. 
• Empower the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) to give 
initial Central level registration and approvals where possible, with a 
view to speeding up the process of project implementation. 
195 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
• Change Government of India's Rules of Business to empower 
Foreign Investment Implementation Authority (FIIA) to expedite the 
processing of administrative and policy approvals. 
• The aggregate FDI target for the Tenth Plan should be disaggregated 
in terms of sectors and relevant administrative 
ministries/departments, to increase accountability. This could help 
ensure that the policy pre-requisites for increasing domestic private 
investment and FDI are expedited by the concerned departments. 
• Sectoral FDI caps should be reduced to the minimum and entry 
barriers eliminated. With the exception of 'Defence Industry*, FDI 
caps can be removed in all manufacturing and mining. Caps can also 
be eliminated in Advertising, Private Banks and Real Estate and 
raised in telecom, Civil Aviation, DTH/KU broadcasting. Insurance 
and Plantations {other than tea). 
• The existing strategy for attracting FDI should be overhauled. The 
relative emphasis must shift from a broad (scatter shot) approach to 
one of targeting specific companies in specific sectors. The Foreign 
Investment Promotion Council (FIPC) should be reformed to 
implement this strategy. It should be chaired by a person with global 
credibility and involve Minister level functionaries w/ho can interact 
with the heads of the Fortune 500 companies. 
• The informational aspects of the strategy should be refined in the 
light of the perceived advantages and disadvantages of India as an 
investment destination and should use information technology and 
modern marketing techniques. 
• the Special Economic Zones should be developed as the most 
competitive destination for export related FDI in the world, by 
simplifying applicable laws, rules and administrative procedures and 
reducing red tape to the levels found in China. The focus should be 
on accelerated/immediate implementation of reforms that may take a 
much longer time [e.g. decade(s)] in the country as a whole and not 
on tax sops. 
• Domestic Policy Reforms in the Power Sector, Urban Infrastructure 
and Real Estate should be expedited to promote private domestic 
and foreign investment.

 2358. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA:

THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): Madam, the Government has given serious 
consideration to the revival of Hindustan Fertilizer Corporation Limited (HFC) 
and Fertilizer Corporation of India Ltd. (FCI). The complexities relating to the 
revival of these Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) arose on account of 
outdated technologies with serious mismatch in equipment, inherent design 
and equipment deficiencies, intrinsic disadvantages in process technology, 
surplus manpov^rer and huge accumulated losses thereby requiring large 
Investments without any commensurate results in terms of sustained and 
viable operations of the plants. 
In May, 2001, a Group of Ministers was constituted to examine the 
comprehensive rehabilitation proposals in respect of the remaining units of 
HFC and FCI. The recommendations of the GoM were considered by the 
Cabinet on ie.7.2002 and 5.9.2002, and it has been decided to close down the 
entire HFC and FCI, excepting its Jodhpur Mining Organisation. While taking 
this decision, the technology as well as feedstock-related issues, in the context 
of cost of production, the likely impact on the Budget and the availability of 
urea in the country were taken into account, Today, only the gas based units 
are financially and functionally efficient and internationally competitive. 
At the time of closure, none of the units of FCI and HFC was in 
operation. The Haldia Fertilizer Project of HFC, though mechanically 
completed in 1979, could never be commissioned. The operations of Durgapur 
unit have remained suspended since 1997. The operations of Barauni unit of 
HFC, and Ramagundam and Talcher units of FCI have been suspended since 
1999. The Gorakhpur unit of FCI was shut down in 1990. The Sindri unit is 
lying closed since March, 2002. Of the various units of HFC and FCI, only the 
Sindri unit of FCI was in production during 1999-2000 to 2001-02 and even 
this unit produced only 0.76 lakh MT during 2001-02 which is equivalent to 
o.38 % of the urea consumption in the country. Thus the production or non-
product ion of urea by the units of FCI and HFC had no significant impact on 
the availability of fertilizers in the country. 
FCI and HFC have been making losses since inception. Their 
accumulated losses as on 31.3.2002 stood at Rs.7,921 crores and Rs.6.725 
crores respectively. The Government has so far extended Plan/non-Plan 
support including equity to these companies amounting to Rs.3,042.28 crores 
and Rs.2,273.75 crores respectively up to 31.3.2002. For 2002-03, a Budgetary 
provision of Rs.i2i crores from FCI and Rs.87 crores for HFC has been made. 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [12 December, 2002] 
In implementation of the decision of the Govemment -- taken on 
5.9.2002 - to close down the entire HFC and FCI, excepting its Jodhpur Mining 
Organisation, these companies have circuiated the Voluntary Separation 
Scheme (VSS) amongst their employees giving them three months' notice to 
avail the scheme failing vi^ich they will be entitled for retrenchment benefits. 
The scheme of VSS is as per the standing  norms of the Department of Public 
Enterprises. The total number of employees as on 30.9.02 are 4.884 in 
respect of HFC and 5,712 in the case of FCI. The expenditure involved for 
VSS is estimated at Rs.301.25 crores fo r HFC and Rs.390 crores for FCI. In 
the normal course, upon closure of the units, the schools, dispensaries etc. 
should be closed and employees be asked to vacate the company quarters 
forthwith. However, taking into consideration the suggestions of the hon. 
Members of Parliament and related employees associations. FCI and HFC 
have decided to extend the following concessions to their employees after 
their release under VSS: 
Permission to retain company quarters till the end of the current 
academic session (April 2003); 
Continuation of the schools and dispensaries (at reduced scales) till 
the end of the current academic session. 
It is also for information that the country is almost self-sufficient in 
urea. Total availability in 2001-02 was 216 lakh MT (inclusive of 2 lakh MT of 
imported urea) and the consumption has been 199 lakh MT. 
In addition, from the year 2005-06 onwards, 16.52 lakh MT of urea 
from Oman-India Fertilizer Company (OMIFCO) is expected to become 
available which the Government is committed to buy back on a predetermined 
long term fixed price. Further, the expansion projects of KRIBHCO at Hazira 
and RCF at Thai are also under consideration. 
So far as availability of urea in different parts of the country, including 
the eastern region, is concerned, supply is ensured to all the States at uniform 
Statutory Sale Price and no State is allowed to suffer from shortage of 
fertilizers. Based on the above, the decision to close HFC and FCI will have no 
impact on the availability of urea in these States. Government will ensure that 
in future also, fertilizers remain available in the various parts of the country 
adequately at uniform price.

TERRORIST ATTACK ON THE PARLIAMENT BUILDING ON 
13TH DECEMBER, 2001 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, th is day, December 13, marks the 
first anniversary of the ghastly terrorist attack on the Parliament House building, 
which shocked not only the entire nation, but also the conscience of all peace 
loving people who cherish democratic values and ethos. It is undoubtedly the 
most audacious and alarming act of terrorism by rtain terrorist outfits who are 
inimical towards our country. The House „alls the heroic deed of our security 
personnel, including two of the -tajya Sabha Secretariat Watch and Ward staff, 
who made the superme crifice, along wi th five Delhi Police Personnel and a 
woman constable or CRPF, to thwart the entry of terrorists inside the 
Parliament House building. In the terrorist attack, one gardener of the CPWD 
also lost his life. We pay our respectful homage to them. Their dedication, 
devotion to duty and timely action had succeeded in averting what could have 
been a  lajo catastrophe. 
Terrorism should be condemned unambiguously. It can be defeated only 
through determination and sustained efforts. On this occasion, we resolve to 
fight terrorism unitedly and with determination tc eliminate it. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of those who lost their lives in that tragedy. 
[Honourable Members then stood in silence for one minute]

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Study of railway bridges 
*341. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Railway staff study bridges abroad" published in the Times of 
India dated the 4th November, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether there was any proposal to send a Railways team 
abroad, to study inspection methods of bridges, as reported; 
(c) if so, whether any team was sent or is being sent; and 
(d) the justification for sending the team? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (d): 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) and (d) Upgradation of technology and modernisation of various 
systems is a continuous ongoing process of Indian Railways. As part of the 
process, presentations were arranged from various firms from abroad on modern 
bridge inspection and management systems. Many of the emerging areas of 
new technologies now being applied in areas like underwater inspection of 
bridges, non-destructive testing of bridges and bridge management systems 
were noted. A proposal to set up a task force to study the needs for upgrading 
and modernisation of bridge inspection and management systems especially 
underwater inspections and non-destructive testing of bridges was mooted in 
March, 2002. The task force was formally set up in September, 2002. Since 
techniques and equipment for such inspections are not available in the country, 
it was considered necessary to study their actual functioning abroad. As a part 
of the terms of reference of task force it was asked to visit countries abroad for 
on the spot study of the systems abroad. The team went abroad for the study tour 
on 3.11.2002 and returned on 28.11.2002.

Boosting to Bio-Technology Sector 
*350. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India is posing for phenomenal growth in Bio-
technology; 
(b) if so, what is the estimated potential of the country; and 
(c) what steps are being taken to give a boost to the Bio-technology 
sector? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The growth of biotechnology has been 
exponential in the last decade with various initiatives taken in public and private 
sector. India has enormous potential to utilize biotechnological tools for increasing 
the productivity and efficiency of agriculture, healthcare, environmental protection 
and industrial sectors. As per the estimates of Confederation of Indian Industry 
(CM), the actual consumption of biotech products during 1999 was about US$ 
1.78 billion and is projected to grow to US$ 4.27 billion by 2010. The biotech 
products in high demand are for human and animal healthcare, agriculture 
including genetically superior seeds, industry and other value added 
recombinant products. With the advent of bioinformatics, genomics and 
proteomics, it is estimated that the growth of this sector will be further 
accelerated covering almost every facet of life. 
Government of India has made concerted efforts to speed up research and 
development, application and commerciali zation of research leads. From Rs. 
622 crore in Ninth Plan (1997—2002), an outlay of Rs.1450 crore for the 
Tenth Plan (2002—07) has been allocated. Further impetus has been provided 
with the establishment of 62 bioinformatics centres, 25 state-of-the-art biotech 
facilities, Centres of Excellence and 64  postgraduate teaching programmes, 
establishment of a National Bioresource Development Board, new institutions 
like National Brain Research Centre, National Centre for Plant Genome Research 
and Institute of Bioresource and Sustainable Development in addition to many 
other national laboratories in frontier areas of biology and biotechnology. 
Significant achievements have been in obtaining research leads, transfer of 
technology, large scale demonstrations and commercialization of 
35 

RAJY ASABHA [13 December, 2002] 
products. Vaccines, diagnostic kits, drug delivery systems and bioremediation 
methods, tissue culture protocols, bio-fertilizers and biopesticides are at various 
stages of development and commercialization. 
To boost the biotech sector for the Biotech Product and Process 
Development, the Government has given various incentives to the biotech industry 
through fiscal measures, custom and ex cise duty exemptions, tax holidays for 
R&D expenditure, encouraging Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), speedy 
clearance of FDI projects by Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), 
constitution of Fast Track Committee (FTC) under Foreign Investment 
Implementation Authority (FIIA) etc. To  inculcate biotech industry in small-
scale sector, a Task Force and a Biotec hnology Cell have been created in the 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Agro and Rural Industries in association 
with Department of Biotechnology. A sensitization programme in the form of 
workshops has jointly been initiated for awareness building in SSI 
entrepreneurs. 
State Governments have taken initiatives to establish biotechnology parks 
and incubators, separate biotech departments and institutes specially to focus on 
local problems. Successful mission projects with biotechnological 
interventions are under implementation in the areas of vaccines, coffee 
improvement, herbal product development and establishment of genomic 
databases. International collaboration has been strengthened with many developed 
and developing countries in the areas of mutual benefit. Research in new areas 
like nanobiology, structural and computational biology has also been initiated. 
The main objective of the above measures is to develop a strong capability in the 
field and harness the potential of biotechnology for societal benefit and economic 
progress.

commits developed countries to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases by an

Melting of Glaciers of Himalayas 
  2396. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Is a blanket of smog chocking South Asia" appearing in the Times 
of India dated the 13th August, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that a recent study by the Delhi University in 
Kullu Valley has revealed that 67 per cent of the 1500 major Glaciers in the 
Himalayas are receding, which could resu lt in abrupt transition in climatic 
conditions, causing rise of 9.88 cm in sea level by 2100 and erosion of low 
lying areas; and 
(c) if so, what is Government's perception about this new phenomenon and the 
steps being contemplated, so that such a situation could be averted? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. An international collaborative study namely, "Indian 
Ocean Research Experiment (INDOEX)" has indicated haze over the Indian Ocean. 
The haze is not a permanent feature of the atmosphere over the Asian region and 
the surrounding seas. It occurs only during January -March, the season in 
which INDOEX observations were made in 1999. The United Nations 
Environment Programme (UNEP) has, this year, brought out a report entitled 
"The Asian Brown Cloud: Climate and other Environmental Impacts" based on 
INDOEX. The press release of the UNEP launching the said report paints an 
alarming picture of the impacts of this baze on both regional and global scales. 
However, most of the concerns expressed therein are not well substantiated by 
reliable modeling studies or experimental observations. 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
(b) The University of Delhi has conducted studies in Kullu Valley on land 
use patterns and not on blanket of smog or on the recession of Himalayan 
Glaciers, sea level rise and erosion of low lying areas. However, according to the 
Geological survey of India, as per the inventory of Himalayan Glaciers, the 
Indian part of Himalaya has more than 7500 glaciers of all dimensions. There 
are only 365 major glaciers more than 5 km in length (excluding Shyok and 
Kishanganga basins). The studies conducted by the Survey reveal that the 
majority of them are receding. The rate of recession in different climate zones of 
Himalaya is found to be variable in different years. Therefore, the studies 
confine to Kullu Valley may not give the overall natural cyclic process. The 
earth has witnessed several phases of glacial and interglacial period. It is a natural 
phenomenon. Presently the earth is passing through an interglacial phase whereby 
the ice bodies throughout the world are receding and the recession of glacier is a 
natural phenomenon and could also be attributed to global warming. 
(c) Regarding smog, it may be mentioned that the existing legal and policy 
framework supported by several initiatives to protect and improve the 
environment, addresses the concerns of air pollution in India. Regarding recession 
of the Himalayan Glaciers, the Govern ment is aware of the environmental 
concerns and has supported conservation activities in the Himalayan region 
including afforestation, establishment of community toilets, and removal of 
garbage and promotion of eco-tourism.

Cotton was effective pest-resistant crop,  was false in the fields of Andhra 
Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra where Bt. Cotton was sown; 
(d) whether the conditional clearance given to Genetically Modified Bt. 
Cotton would be withdrawn, in the light of above facts;

GM crop? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes Sir; The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee 
(GEAC) accorded conditional clearance for introduction of three Bt. cotton 
hybrids namely BT MECH 162, BT MECH 184, BT MECH 12 into the 
environment for a period of three years from April 2002 to March 2005. The 
conditions, inter-alia, include plantation of a non-Bt refuge around the periphery 
of the Bt fields equivalent to five rows of non_Bt cotton variety or 20% of the 
total sown area, monitoring the susceptibility of bollworms to Bt gene vis-a-vis 
baseline susceptibility data by an agency identified by the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests, undertaking studies on possible impacts on non-target 
insects and crops, developing plans for Bt based Integrated Pest Management, 
developing and depositing with the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Research 
(NBPGR), the DNA fingerprints of the 
84 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
approved varieties and undertaking of an awareness and education 
programme for farmers. 
(c) The three approved hybrid varieties are presently under cultivation only 
in six states namely Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Some of the fields where these hybrid 
varieties are being cultivated have recently been monitored by the Committees 
constituted by this Ministry for each state. The Committees found the 
performance of Bt. Cotton satisfactory. 
(d) There is no proposal from the Government to ban the sale of Bt Cotton 
seeds in India.

commercial cultivation of transgenic mustard. The GEAC in the 34th Meeting 
held on 7th November, 2002 considered the proposal but no final decision was 
taken.

gene (s), biochemical characterization of the expressed proteins, estimation of 
level of expressed proteins, safety of the expressed proteins to the non-target 
organisms, environmental fate of expressed proteins, pollen escape, 
outcrossing, aggressiveness and weediness, effect on non-target organisms, 
confirmation of the absence of Terminator Gene, and baseline susceptibility 
studies and agronomic, compositional and food and feed safety evaluation of 
transgenic hybrids as compared to the non-transgenic counterpart.

Trading of Indian Saras 
2419. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of ENVIORNMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that trading of Indian Saras, the State bird of Uttar 
Pradesh, is prohibited under the Wildlife Protection Act; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that there are only 8000 Saras all over the 
world, of which 6000 are in Uttar Pradesh, but these are much on sale in the 
market of Lucknow; and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken by Government to rescue the bird, 
for conservation? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, sir.

estimated total population of Saras in the world is 8000-10,000, out of which

regarding sale of Saras in the market of Lucknow but these have not been 
confirmed on investigation. However, to prevent any sale of Saras cranes 
constant vigil is kept by the field staff.

Commercial production of GM Mustard 
†2422. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHAR DA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any proposal to permit Genetically Modified (GM) Mustard, 
prepared by mixing five types of foreign genes, for commercial production, is 
under Government's consideration; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when a final decision in this regard is likely to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) No, Sir. The transgenic hybrid mustard developed by M/s. 
Proagro Seed Company Ltd. for improving the yield contain three genes for 
three traits; these are (i) bar (glucosinolate ammonium tolerance trait), (ii) bamase 
(male sterility producing trait), and (iii) barstar (restoration of fertility trait). Based 
on the recommendation of the Monitoring-cum-Evaluation Committee (MEC) 
of the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and Review Committee on Genetic 
Manipulation (RCGM), the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) 
in its 27th Meeting held on 8th August, 2001 permitted M/s. Proagro Seeds 
Company Ltd. to conduct large scale open field trials. Subsequently the 
Company submitted the proposal for approval of the GEAC for commercial 
release and marketing of transgenic mustard and seed production.The GEAC has 
not given the approval as yet. 
GM Mustard 
2423. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN:            
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have given approval for genetically modified 
mustard being marketed in the country; 
(b) if so, whether an evaluation has been made of the benefits of higher 
productivity vis-a-vis the risks to health and local varieties; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether the insect-resistant Bt. Cotton crop has been found to be 
successful; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) 
114 

 
[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
in its 27th Meeting held on 8th August, 2001 permitted M/s. Proagro Seeds 
Company Ltd. Gurgaon to conduct large scale open field trials only. The 
company has been involved in the research and development of transgenic hybrids 
of Indian mustard for improving the yield for the last three years, following 
Department of Biotechnology guidelines. During the field trials the hybrids 
have been tested and compared with the non-transgenic hybrid for various 
parameters. It has been found that the hybrids offered better agronomic 
performance over the best available varieties in the country. Subsequently, the 
request of the company to allow for commercial release and marketing of 
transgenic mustard and seed production was considered by the GEAC in the 34th 
Meeting held on 7th November, 2002.The GEAC has decided to further examine 
the data submitted by the company. 
(d) and (e) Bt Cotton an insect resistant variety hybrid developed by 
Maharashtra Hybrid Seed Company (MAHYCO) is the first and only 
transgenic crop approved by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) 
for commercial cultivation in India.The GEAC accorded conditional approval for 
release of three Bt Cotton hybrid varieties namely BT MECH 162, BT MECH 
184 and BT MECH 12 into the environment after taking into consideration the 
reports of large scale field trials on Bt Cotton varieties and recommendations of the 
Monitoring Evaluation Committee constituted by the Department of 
Biotechnology and Indian Council for Agricultural Research and Biosafety 
evaluation. Some of the fields where these hybrid varieties are being cultivation 
have recently been monitored by a Committee constituted by this Ministry. The 
Committee found the performance of Bt. Cotton satisfactory in terms of higher 
number of bolls, reduced number of sprays for control of bollworms and higher 
yields in the cotton harvested so far.

Admission in engineering and medical science studies 
2436. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that non-Government institutions, 
conducting professional courses generally take huge amount from the 
124 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
students seeking admission in engineering and medical science studies; 
(b) what sort of control Government are maintaining over such 
institutions; 
(c) whether Government are planning to increase the in-take capacity of 
Government sponsored professional colleges, to admit students in more number; 
and 
(d) if so, the details of such plants? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (d) 
Engineering Education 
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has constituted 
various State Level Fee Committees for fixing Fees to be charged by self-
financing technical institutions. The State level fee committee consist of Vice 
Chancellor of a University in the Stat e, Secretaries of the Department of 
Technical Education and Department of Finance, two economist or experts in 
cost accountancy with back ground of institutional finance and Member 
Secretary not below the rank of Joint Secretary or director of the State 
Government. All the self-financing institutions are bound by the fees structure 
prescribed by the Fee Committees and ar e not allowed to charge excess fees, 
capitation fees or donation for the purpose of admission from the students. The 
concerned state government are supposed to monitor the technical institutions. 
Whenever such cases of overcharging of the fees and collection of capitation 
and donations from the students come to the notice of the AICTE, appropriate 
actions are taken against such institutions after conducting necessary 
investigations into such matters. 
2. Technical institutions are expected to follow norms and standards 
prescribed by the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE). This also 
includes fees structure prescribed by State Level Fee Committees. If a technical 
institution does not do so, punitive acti on such as putting it under 'Reduced 
Intake' or 'No Admission' category may be taken. 
3. AICTE has not made any plan for increase in intake for Government aided 
Professional Colleges in technical education. However, if a technical institution 
submits application to AICTE for increase in intake of seats 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
the same is considered by AICTE as per laid down procedure and norms & 
standards. 
Medical Science 
1. With a view to prevent the commercialization of medical colleges, and 
also to prevent private medical colleges from charging capitation fees, the 
Supreme Court of India in the Case of Unnikrishnan J.R versus State, evolved a 
scheme for regulating admissions in private medical colleges. As per the 
scheme, 50% of the total seats are to be merit seats, 35% payment seats and the 
remaining 15% earmarked for NRI/Foreign students in all the private medical 
colleges, except for minority colleges. The admission fo the first two categories 
i.e. merit and payment seats is to be made by the competent authority in the 
respective States, on the basis of merit to be determined either on the basis of a 
competitive entrance test or the merit determined in the qualifying examination. 
In minority medical colleges, 50% seats are filled through the competent 
authority of the respective State Government and remaining 50% filled by the 
management on the basis of merit amongst the candidates belonging to the 
concerned minority. Since merit is the sole criteria for obtaining admissions, 
hard-working and meritorious students have benefited by the scheme evolved by 
the Supreme Court. As regards the fee st ructure, this had been fixed by the 
Supreme Court for the period 1993-94 to 1996-97. Subsequently, the Central 
Government has been fixing the upper ceiling of the fee for merit and payment 
seats in private medical college and within this upper ceiling, the fees in each 
medical college is being fixed by the respective State Government. No fee has. 
however, been prescribed by the Central Government for 15% seats earmarked 
for NRI/Foreign students. The eleven Judge Bench of Supreme Court of India had 
recently given a judgment on admission and fee in aided and unaided medical 
institution. 
2. At present there is no proposal to increase the intake capacity. 
However, any applicant fulfilling the eligibility and qualifying criteria 
prescribed in the regulations "The Opening of a New or Higher Course of Study or 
Training (including Post-graduate Course of Study or Training) and Increase of 
Admission Capacity in any Course of Study or Training (including a Post-
graduate Course of Study or Training) Regulations, 2000" brought out by the 
Medical Council of India, can apply for permission to 
126 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the Central Government for increase  in admission capacity in medical 
colleges.

2456. SHRI R.RGOENKA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Expenditure Reforms Commission, in its 
recent report, has highlighted, inter-alia, that the universities are steadily losing 
primacy in the research and development efforts in the country, due to poor 
funding by the University Grants Commission; and 
(b) if so, the details of the major observations/recommendations of the 
Commission and the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon, so as to 
improve the standards of teaching and research in universities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMAJ: (a) Yes, 
Sir. In this respect ERC in its recent report has made the following 
observations: 
"The UGC has responsibility for extending assistance for both standards 
of teaching and for research. However, within the resources available to the 
UGC, the share of research is a small fraction. Apart from other equally 
valid reasons, this situation is also responsible for universities steadily 
losing primacy in the R&D effort in the country." 
144 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b)The major recommendations ma de by the Expenditure Reforms 
Commission in its recent report, inter-alia, are: (i) there is a need to develop in-
house academic expertise in the UGC, (ii) the responsibility for determination 
and disbursement of maintenance grant to Delhi Colleges should be transferred 
along with the funds to the appropri ate agency designated by the State 
Government of Delhi, (iii) there is a need to review a large number of programmes 
initiated by UGC so as to ensure that the meager funds available with the UGC 
are not thinly spread over a large number of activities, (iv) UGC should seek to 
enhance the resources to be allocated for 'research' out of the total funds and find 
better means to optimally utilize these funds by devising result-oriented 
approach and (v) UGC should take steps to promote the quality in the 
universities and colleges and establish linkages between the accreditation of the 
institutions with the release of the grants etc. 
The UGC is in agreement with the general recommendations of the ERC 
for the increased funding in research. However, the disbursement of grants to the 
universities and colleges for different programmes, including research projects 
depends on the quantum of funds made available to the UGC. Despite the 
financial constraints the research has been a prime concern of the UGC. The 
UGC has been providing assistance to universities/colleges and individual 
teachers for research under its different schemes, which include: 
1. Teaching and research in interdisciplinary areas. 
2. Assistance for Strengthening of Infrastructure in Science and

Pre-Harappan civilization 
2465. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Institute of Ocean Technology had 
indicated a likely Pre-Harappan civilization; 
(b) if so, what is the basis for the exploration; and 
(c) what further steps have been taken to conduct research in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b)The Natio nal Institute of Ocean Technology 
(NIOT), Chennai of the Department of Ocean Development (DOD) 
Government of India had during the course of under water surveys in the Gulf of 
Cambay, Gujarat during Cctober, 2000 to March, 2001 come across a stretch of 
formations typical of a riverine regime in the middle of the sea at 30—40 m. 
water depth. An area of almost 9km. Stretch west of Hazira in Gujarat appeared 
to be lined with well laid house basement like feature 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
partially covered by sand waves and sand ripples. The Side Scan Sonar deployed 
for the survey picked up images which indicate several geometric objects that are 
normally man made. 
During subsequent surveys in November-December, 2001 various objects 
were picked up from the sea bed. Among the objects collected, the carbonized 
wood pieces were taken up for dating using C14 technique in the Birbal Sahni 
Institute of Palaeo Botany, Lucknow and in National Geophysical Research 
Institute, Hyderabad. The preliminary results reveal that the age of the w ood 
samples dated back to 7500 B.C. This has been further substantiated by dating 
carried out at laboratories in Germany. 
These results and some of the objects collected were made public in a 
Press Conference on 16th January, 2002. Further detailed surveys, studies and 
investigations would need to be done in the area by multi-disciplinary, multi-
institutional teams to conclusively establish the period of settlement. 
(c) As a follow up, a workshop was organized on 1 st July 2002 at NIOT 
campus, Chennai which was attended by about 50 eminent personalities 
belonging to different fields like archaeology, geology, geo-morphology, geo-
chronology and marine technology. Based on the recommendations in the 
workshop, several organisations and institutions were asked to give proposal 
pertaining to the expertise that will be of importance to the gulf of Cambay 
marine archeological findings.

2466. SHRI R.P. GOEN KA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state:

conduct inquiries into major rail accidents, cannot function independently and 
impartially, as they are dependent on the Ministry of Railways for all their 
important requirements, like office and residential accommodation, transport 
and other perks for their officers, as well as for submitting their findings on 
accidents to the Railway board;

independent statutory authority status for the Chief Commissioner of Railway 
Safety; and 
156 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the comparative set up obtaining in some other countries like 
Britain, USA etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) The Commissioners of Railway Safety, 
whose one of the many functions is to conduct inquiries into serious rail 
accidents, are entitled to get infrastructure support viz. accommodation, 
transport, etc. from the Ministry of Railways. They are, however, independent 
of the Ministry of Railways as their budget, appointment, promotion, pay & 
allowances etc. are under the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The fac ilities being 
provided by the Railways are as per the service conditions agreed by the 
Ministry of Railways.They function independently and impartially in conducting 
accident inquiries and finalising their reports. 
The accident inquiry reports are fina lly submitted to the Ministry of 
Railways, as the Railway Board is the safety controlling authority and they 
examine and implement the accepted recommendations, made by the 
Commissioners. 
(b) Railway Safety Review Committee (1998) has also supported the 
independent nature and status of the Commission of Railway Safety. 
(c) In USA, National Transport Safety Board (NTSB) is an independent 
Federal agency charged with investig ation in every major accident of all 
transportation sectors. In Britain, the functions of Railway Safety Inspectorate 
called the "Her Majesty's Safety Inspector ate" are broadly similar to that of 
Commission of Railway Safety in India.

SHRI U.V. KRISHNAM RAJU: Sir, concerns have been raised by 
hon. Members in regard to the poisonous effects on wheat, rice, sugar and 
other food items on being packed in plastic bags for a long duration of time. 
It may be recalled that the Government of India have approved the 
road map for dilution of the compulsory packaging norms laid down under the 
Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 
1987 in respect of foodgrains in July 2002. This has been done with a view to 
enabling the jut® industry to become cost and quality competitive in domestic 
and international markets. The cumulative percentages of dilution for 
foodgrains for the Jute Year (July to June) 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 are 20% 
and 40% respectively. The percentages of reservation for packaging in jute 
bags will, therefore, be 80% and 60% for foodgrains for the 1 st and 2 nd year 
respectively. The position will be reviewed in the 3rd year. 
The Indian Grain Storage Managem ent and Research Institute 
(IGSMRI), Hapur, a research and development institution of the Department of 
Food and Public Distribution has conduc ted a scientific stud y to evaluate the 
suitability of PP/HDPE bags for the storage of foodgrains under field 
conditions. The study was conducted in different agro-climatic zones at Food 
Storage' Depots (FSD) of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) situated at Delhi, 
Shahjahanpur (UP). Cherlapally & Samalkot (AP), Kollam (Kerala), 
Bhubaneswar (Orissa), Jallandhar (Punjab), Una (HP), Rampur (MP) and 
Jorhat (Assam) for different commodities like wheat and rice. 
On the basis of the study, the IGSMRI has found that: 
(I)    PP/ HDPE bags are light in weight as compared to jute bags. 
00   PP/ HDPE bags are cheaper as compared to jute bags. 
(iii)   Prophylactic and curative treatment against stored grain insect 
pests is effective. 
The IGSMRI conducted its res earch study for one year storage 
period and has recommended that: 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2003] 
"PP/HDPE antislip bags can be used for storage of foodgrains by 
State procuring agencies in a phased ma nner, preferably to begin with the 
operational stocks in covered godowns at safe moisture level". 
The Indian Institute of Technolo gy (IIT), New Delhi has also 
conducted studies on the use of PP/HDPE bags for packaging of foodgrains 
and other items and found that Plastic Woven Sacks (PWS) made of HDPE or 
PP outperform their traditional counter parts (jute and paper bags) due to 
superiority exhibited in the following key functional areas : 
Low seepage loss, yet option of breathing requirement not sacrificed. 
Moisture resistant: hence most suitable packaging for hygroscopic 
substances like, fertilizer and sugar. 
Water and insect resistant, thus allowing the PP-HDPE bags to be 
stored in warehouses and godowns wi thout fear of deterioration and 
subsequent wastage. 
The Indian Council of Medical Rese arch (ICMR) on the basis of a 
study conducted by the National Institut e of Nutrition (NIN), Hyderabad has 
indicated that, as per available informat ion, food items like grains and flours 
can be safely stored in plastic bags. However, conditions like initial moisture 
content, inoculum potential of biolog ical agents like insects and fungi, 
conditions of storage including temp erature and humidity, surrounding 
hygiene, and frequency of fumigation ha ve considerable bearing on the 
stability of the product and these vary according to the type of agricultural 
commodity. 
The Bureau of Indian Standards  (BIS) has standardised the 
specifications of PP / HDPE woven sacks for packaging of foodgrains and 
sugar. The BIS have indicated that the standards on HDPE/PP bags for 
packing of foodgrains and sugar have been issued after due consideration of 
health and safety aspects. The packaging of cereals and sugar is governed by 
the various BIS specifications, wherein the requirement of the overall migration 
limit (combination of all those constitu ents which adversely affect health) has 
been prescribed. It has, inter alia, been prescribed that foodgrains and sugar 
should be packed only in woven sacks made of 
218 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
specific materials, which are reasonably safe for personal health. The BIS 
specifications of textiles - High De nsity Poly Ethyelene (HDPE) / Poly 
Propylene (PP) woven sacks for packaging foodgrains and sugar (No. IS 
14887 : 2000 & 14968 : 2001) prescribes that the raw material for the tape 
shall be manufactured from virgin High Density Poly Ethyelene (HDPE) / Poly 
Propylene (PP) conforming to requirements specified in IS: 10146 or IS: 10910 
respectively. The BIS have stated that  the aforesaid Indian Standards on 
plastic raw materials for use in contact with food items are based on 
internationally accepted requirements such as European Norms, US PDA 
Regulations. British Plastic Federation Report, London etc. on the subject. The 
BIS have further informed that for ensur ing quality of bags in terms of long 
term stability to prevent degradation durin g use, the use of UV stabilized raw 
materials has been specified in the standards listed in the above 
specifications. 
As per available information, PP bags for packing of sugar are being 
used in Indonesia. Malaysia, Middle East, Brazil, Cuba, and E.U. countries. 
The Directorate General of Health  Services have intimated that 
plastic bags manufactured out of the plastic packaging materials enlisted 
under Rule 49(5)(v) of Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules. 1955 are 
safe to pack foodgrains and sugar if the material used for manufacturing 
HDPE / PP bags conforms to the specifications prescribed by BIS. 
It may be mentioned that PP/HDPE woven sacks are produced from 
the same raw materials which are used in items of daily human consumption 
(in India as well as in other countries) such as milk, edible oils, consumer packs 
of rice, sugar, wheat, tea, coffee, flour, salt, spices and pulses. The items most 
sensitive to human health, such as medicines, life saving drugs, blood and 
plasma pouches are all packed in articles of PP/HDPE and other plastic raw 
materials. No report or incidence of poisonous effect of PP/HDPE bags during 
storage of foodgrains has so far come to Government's notice. 
In the light of the facts mentio ned above, health hazards do not 
appear to be involved in the use of PP/HDPE bags for packing of foodgrains 
and sugar. The Food Corporation of India (FCI) is yet to take decision   on   
the   procurement   of  PP/HDPE   bags   for   the   storage   of

foodgrains will be considered carefully befor e decision on the use of PP /

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Ban on Animal Testing 
*361. SHRI MUNAVVAR HASAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that production of anti-snake venom has been 
stopped; 
(b) whether ban on animal testing is creating hurdles in research and 
development efforts of Pharmaceutical companies in the country; 
(c) if so, the manner in which the companies are now supposed tc test the 
new medicines; and 
(d) the action proposed to help the Indian companies which are 
compelled to plan-animal testing abroad? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) In view of restrictions placed by the Committee for the 
Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) 
functioning under the Ministry of Environment and Forests in the procurement 
of horses and certain other procedural matters, the production of Anti-Snake Venom 
Serum (ASVS) has been stopped where the bleeding of horses of the age of 21 and 
above was done. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been taking up 
the matter with CPCSEA and the Ministry of Environment and Forests in order to 
resolve the issues so that the production of the serum and drug research can be 
resumed at the earliest for ensuring adequate availability of ASVS and furthering 
research and development in drugs. 
Development of new drug requires extensive animal studies both at the 
stage of research as well as to determine its possible toxicity, efficacy 
1 

RAJYA  SABHA [16 December, 2002] 
and mechanism of action. Such animal testing is a mandatory requirement 
throughout the world, including the regulatory provisions under Drugs & 
Cosmetics Act of India, and as such testing the drug without animal 
experimentation is not feasible. Representations have been received to the effect 
that the restrictive provisions of Breeding and Experiments on Animals 
(Control and Supervision) Rules and its modalities of CPCSEA in its 
implementation like ban on import of animals except genetically defined rats 
and mice, ban on contract research, procurement of animals from registered 
breeders only and delay in granting permission for experiments on larger 
animals has made it very dificult for research based drug industry to undertake 
drug development, thus losing their competitive edge in the international 
scenario. 
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has already taken up with the 
concerned authorities the issue of protecting the medical research including 
drug development as envisaged in Section 14 of Prevention of Cruelty to 
Animals Act, 1960.

Vacancies in High Courts 
*372. SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
24 

[16 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of total sanctioned strength of 647 judges 
in country's 21 High Courts, over 150 posts of judges are still lying vacant; 
(b) whether this is the main reason for mounting of cases pending with 
the various courts in the country; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that  neither the Law Commission's 
recommendations nor the repeated reminders of successive Chief Justices of the 
apex court have resulted in raising the strength of judges in the judiciary; and 
(d) if so, the reasons for delay in implementing the recommendations of the 
Law Commission in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Against the approved strength of 647 Judges in 21 High Courts, 
505 Judges were in position as on 12.12.2002 leaving 142 vacancies to be 
filled up. While every efforts is made  to fill up the existing vacancies 
expeditiously, vacancies do keep arising on account of retirement, resignation 
or elevation of Judges. Government has been periodically reminding the Chief 
Justices of High Courts, the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Ministers of the 
States to initiate proposals for filling up all vacant posts of Judges in the High 
Courts. They have been reminded last on October 28,2002. 
The pendency of cases in Courts could be ascribed to various factors which, 
inter-alia, include vacancies of judges, increase in fresh institution of cases, rise 
in population, heightened awareness of rights on the part of the citizens, granting 
of adjournments, industrial development in the country, increase in trade and 
commerce and socio-economic matters, legislative and administrative aspects 
touching on the lives of citizens, lawyers' strike etc. 
The Law Commission in its 14th Report on Reform of Judicial 
Administration (1958) recommended that the strength of Judges of High Courts 
be fixed on the basis of the average annual institution of all types 
25 

RAJYA  SABHA [16 December, 2002] 
of proceedings in a particular High Court during the previous three years and the 
strength so fixed should be reviewed at an interval of two or three years. The 
Supreme Court in their judgement in the Supreme Court Advocates-On-
Record Association and Anr. v/s. Union of India, has held that it is necessary to 
make a periodic review of the Judge strength of every High Court with 
reference to the felt need for disposal of cases, taking into account the backlog 
and the expected future filing. The meeting of the Chief Ministers of the States 
and the Chief Justices of the High Courts on Decembe r 4, 1993 resolved that 
for effectively dealing with arrears of pending cases, the Government should 
undertake review of the optimum strength of the Judges in each High Court once 
in three years, in consultation with the constitutional functionaries in the States 
concerned and the Chief Justice of India.  Accordingly, the Judge strength is 
reviewed every three years. The judge strength was last reviewed in 1999 and 
43 posts of judges were approved in various High Courts. The next review, due 
in 2002, would be completed shortly. 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: Sir, in firs t half of the statement, it is 
stated: "Against the approved strength of 647 Judges in 21 High Courts, 505 
Judges were in position as on 12.12. 2002, leaving 142 vacancies to be f illed 
up", that is, about one-fourth. Then, in the last sentence says "The next 
review, due in 2002, would be completed shortly". When you were talking of a 
review, was this figure of 12.12.2002 in your mind or you are talking of an 
independent review? Could you please clarify? 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, as far as the review of judges' 
strength is concerned, it is done every three years. But, as far as appointment in 
regard to the existing vacancies is c oncerned, this year, we have already 
appointed 74 judges to different High Courts. As of now, 70 vacancies are in the 
process of being filled up. Those are completely independent. As far as the 
review part is concerned, you have to get feedback from the judges, the Chief 
Justices of various High Courts, the State Governments, and then you have to 
take a structured view. This is going on and it will be completed shortly. 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: No, Sir, I am somewhat confused. The hon. 
Minister is a very bright young man. Here he says that there are 142 vacancies, 
as on 12.12.2002. But you just now said that there are 70 vacancies. The other 
thing is that, the next review is due in 2002. Today, it is 16th of December. Is 
the review completed or is it still due? 
26 

[16 December. 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, Shri Natwar Singh is a very 
senior hon. Member. I think he would understand. We have said very clearly 
in our reply "it will be completed shortly". This review is a comprehensive 
process wherein we have to consult the State Governments, the hon. Chief 
Justices of different High Courts. We have to see the workload. All these things 
will come to a structured view. It will be done shortly. 
SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. Has the hon. 
Minister considered that one cause of delay, apart from all these vacancies, 
etc., could be remedied by resorting to ad hoc appointment of Judges, which our 
Constitution permits? Therefore, when a Judge of a High Court retires at the 
age of 62—his age of retirement is known—it is possible, if you can't 
immediately find a suitable person and fill up the vacancy, to allow that 
particular person to continue on ad hoc basis so that there would be no vacancy 
as such, until you find a suitable person. 
The second point, which I have suggested repeatedly to the Chief 
Justices of India and the Law Minist ers, is that competent people and 
practitioners, in large cities, will be willing to accept appointments on ad hoc 
basis, even for two or three years, at the request of the Law Minister, and they

SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir,  Shri Nariman is one of the 
most respected jurists in the country and his views are entitled to respect. As of 
now, judicial appointment is done through a consultation process where the 
entire matter is initiated by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. After

entire appointment process.Therefore, there is a consultation process of the 
Collegium of the High Court followed by the Collegium of the Supreme Court 
in the entire process. 
As far as appointment of Judges on ad hoc basis is concerned, it is a matter 
for the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court to initiate. If the matter is 
initiated by the Chief Justice concerned, the Government would certainly 
suitably reply to it. It is a matter for review or consideration. 
As far as the question relating to appointment of bright young lawyers or 
good lawyers is concerned, it is again a matter which will be given

Sex-determination tests 
*376 PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has recently  directed the States to take 
action against clinics which resort to sex-determination advertisements; 
(b) if so, the action taken by his Ministry; 
(c) whether his Ministry has evolved any mechanism to stop such 
clinics from giving publicity to sex-determination tests; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. While hearing a PIL (Writ 
Petition No. 301 of 2000 filed by CEHAT and Others v/s Union of India and 
Others) on 7.10.2002, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, inter-alia, stated that the 
learned counsel for the petitioners has pointed out that some of the States/UTs 
particularly the States of Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi are not 
stopping the advertisements in the newspaper issued by some clinics for 
carrying out sex-determination and/or abortion. Therefore, the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court directed the competent authorities of the States/UTs to take 
appropriate action against such clinics. 
Advertisements regarding facilities of pre-natal determination of sex of 
unborn child are prohibited under Sec tion 22 of the Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of  Misuse) Act, 1994. The Act also 
prescribes punishments for contravening its provisions with imprisonment 
upto 5 years and fine upto Rs. 50,000/- 
Since implementation of the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 rests with States/UTs., all the 
States/UTs have been advised to take action as per the directions of the Court

News-item "India loses WTO cases against European Union" 
2520.   PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: 
SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "India loses WTO case against European Union", which appeared in 
the 'Indian Express', dated the 6th November, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and how would Government defend WTO cases 
in future; 
(c) if so, the detailed study undertaken in this regard; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) to (d) India had resorted to 
World Trade Organization's (WTO) Dispute Settlement Mechanism and 
challenged the anti-dumping duty imposed by European Communities (EC) on 
imports of bed linen from India. On 12 March, 2001 the Dispute Settlement 
Body (DSB) adopted the Appellate Body Report and the Penal Report as modified 
by the Appellate Body, in this dispute. These Reports concluded that the EC's 
imposition of definitive anti-dumping duties on imports of cotton-type bed linen 
from India had been inconsistent with the Anti-dumping Agreement. Pursuant to 
the recommendations of these Reports, the DSB requested the European 
Communities to bring its measures into conformity with its obligations under 
the Anti-dumping Agreement. Subsequently EC undertook a review of the 
anti-dumping measure and re-determined the level of anti-dumping duty. 
However, the application of the duty was suspended. India strongly disagreed 
with the re-determination and at its request a Compliance Panel had been constituted 
52 

[16 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
to examine the consistency of measures taken by EC in compliance with the 
decision of the DSB in the origin al bed linen dispute with EC. The 
Compliance Panel has concluded that EC has implemented the 
recommendations of the DSB in the original bed linen dispute. The 
Compliance Panel Report would be adopted by the DSB unless a party to the 
dispute decides to appeal the report or the DSB decides by consensus not to adopt 
the Report.The Government is considering the future course of action in this 
dispute in accordance with the rules of the WTO. 
In respect of the disputes in whic h the DSB has adopted the panel and 
Appellate Body reports, India has won 5 cases and also lost 5 eases. In one case 
India requested termination of the panel proceedings in light of the removal by 
the United States of the disputed safeguard measure. Government has been 
pursuing WTO cases in coordination with concerned administrative Ministries, 
Department of Legal Affairs and the legal experts engaged for the disputes. For 
each dispute a lawyer is appointed with the prior approval of Department of 
Legal Affairs. Where necessary an ex perienced foreign lawyer is also 
appointed with the approval of the Department of Legal Affairs.

A straight comparison between India and China on the basis of WIR02

respect of both India and China is based on national official sources and not 
in accordance with international standards stipulated in the Balance of 
Payments Manual (5th Edition) published by the IMF. Whereas the FDl data 
in respect of India as reported in the WIR02 is based on RBI reporting, which 
only takes into account direct investment in equity and preference capital and 
does not take into consideration reinvested earnings and other direct capital 
flows (which actually should form part  of FDl as per IMF definition), the

render a proper comparison difficult. Notwithstanding the above, the higher 
level of FDl inflows into China is mainly due to the fact that China had 
opened up more than a decade before India did, which has enabled, it to attain 
the critical mass and benefit from its spillover effects. The other factors 
responsible for the strong performance of China on the FDl front include the 
Hong Kong-Taiwan advantage, huge infrastructure spending by Government, 
etc.

Impact of globalisation on tea industry 
2528. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the impact of globalisation of future of tea industry in India; 
(b) the reasons for sudden decline of tea market and action taken by the 
Government to rescue the tea producers especially the small tea growers; 
(c) the details of financial and technical assistance provided to tea growers as 
a relief package, fixation of minimum su pport price, re-sch edulement of loan, 
interest relief etc.; and 
(d) the special packages taken by Tea Board, if any, in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI):  (a) With the lifting of quan titative 
restrictions on imports since April 2001, the domestic economy has been integrated 
with the world economy. Though imports of tea have increased, this has not had any 
significant impact on the domestic tea i ndustry as such imports constitute only 
about 2% of the domestic production of tea. Besides, more than 95% of the 
imported tea is re-exported after blending with Indian tea. However, to protect 
against any future surge in imports, the import duty on tea has been increased from 
70% to 100% in 2002-03. 
(b) to (d) The tea growers in India are presently facing problems due 
to the decline in the prices of tea. This coupled with lower growth rate of 
domestic demand and higher cost of production, has adversely affected 
the tea industry including the small growers.  
Government has taken several measures to assist the tea sector and make it 
more competitive in the liberalized regime. These measures include: 
64 

[16 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
• Tea Board is implementing a quality upgradation programme in the 
country, for improving the quality of tea produced by small growers. 
• Financial and technical incentives are being provided by Tea Board 
under its Plan Schemes for development activities like replantation, 
rejuvenation and modernization of tea factories. 
• A Factory Upgradation Scheme has been implemented by the Tea 
Board to encourage the production of good quality orthodox and non-
reconditioned Cut-Tear-Curl (CTC) teas in the country. 
• RBI has announced in August, 2002, a relief package which 
provides for restructuring/re-schedulement of the loans outstanding 
in the tea sector from the commercial banks, etc. 
• The allowance under Section 33AB of Income Tax Act has been 
increased from 20% to 40% in the Budget for 2001 -02. 
• Excise duty on tea has been reduced from Rs. 2 per kg. to Re.1 per 
kg in the Budget for 2002-03. 
• Tea Marketing (Control) Order, 1984 has been modified to remove the 
condition of obligatory sale of 75% of tea production through public 
tea auctions. The producers of tea are now free to sell their teas 
anywhere. 
• Tea Board is implementing a Medium Term Export Strategy on tea in 
close coordination with the tea industry. As a part of this strategy, a 
communication campaign to promote Indian tea and the Logo 
developed by the Tea Board was launched in Russia in October, 2002. 
• Government has also provided financial incentives to exporters of tea 
for meeting a part of cost of handling, packaging, transport/ freight 
charges. 
• Sale of tea in the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) by 100% Export 
Oriented Units (EOUs) and units in Export Processing Zones 
(EPZs) is banned. 
• A generic promotion campaign has been launched for improving the 
consumption of tea within the country. 
65 

RAJYA  SABHA [16 December, 2002] 
• Government has also decided to establish a Price Stabilisation Fund 
(PSF) for providing relief to the grow ers of tea, coffee, rubber and 
tobacco.
